The collective will cease to suppress the individual personality and will instead give it complete freedom to develop internally.
The dialectic will then take place within the individual person rather than within a collective distinct from individuals—society, “class,” or the state—as it did during properly historical periods.
And this also changes the character of the Phenomenology.

During a historical period, the human and natural world did not “appear” to individuals directly. It appeared to them primarily insofar as they were representatives of a particular class or society, or representatives of a state.
The world therefore “appeared,” so to speak, to a collective through an individual who was essentially the representative of that collective.
The phenomena described in a socialist Phenomenology can therefore be called collective “appearances” or collective phenomena.
Here the dialectical interdependence exists only between collective phenomena.
Under communism, by contrast, phenomena will be individual.
Dialectical relations will exist between persons as such, including between the different ways in which the natural and human worlds “appear” to those persons.
The specific content of a communist Phenomenology will therefore consist precisely in describing these individual phenomena and their dialectical development.

In other words, the socialist Phenomenology is “definitive” in the sense that it gives an exact and exhaustive description of all collective appearances—that is, all properly historical, social, and political appearances.
And it is precisely because of this objective completeness that it can be circular in the second sense described above.
It returns to “sensation” because sensation is the first collective phenomenon: it belongs to human beings in general, not merely to some single, unique individual.
And the fact that the Phenomenology necessarily returns to sensation shows that its “end”—that is, the Phenomenology itself—is nothing other than the final collective “appearance.”
It belongs not only to its author but to the whole age—to the entire socialist collective whose representative the author is and whose “recognition” he therefore requires.
A genuinely “definitive,” absolutely true, communist Phenomenology would therefore divide naturally into two basic parts.
The first would give an exhaustive description of all collective phenomena. The second would give an exhaustive description of all individual phenomena.
And the first part would be nothing other than our socialist Phenomenology.

So because the socialist Phenomenology would survive as a true constituent part of the final Phenomenology, it can itself be regarded as definitive or true: the object proper to it has been completely exhausted.
Of course, “wisdom” will be reached only under communism.
In other words, it is only for the “communist” author of the Phenomenology that actuality will cease to “appear,” from his own point of view, and will instead simply be “given” as it truly is.
When he says “for us,” he will genuinely be able to add: “that is, in itself.”

What he says about an actuality “appearing” to a consciousness he describes will no longer itself be merely a description of how that actuality “appears” to his own consciousness. It will be a description of actuality itself.
And from his point of view, the socialist phenomenologist will be seen as occupying the standpoint of a consciousness to which reality still “appears” rather than being directly “given.”
In that sense, he will be able to say that the circle of the socialist Phenomenology exhausts only the possibilities of its author, not of actuality itself.
But the capacities of the author of the socialist Phenomenology coincide with the capacities of humanity insofar as humanity belongs to history.
In other words, absolutely everything that can “appear” to human beings during history in the strict sense appears to this author.
So if the socialist Phenomenology is an “appearance,” or if you prefer an “ideology,” it is the appearance or ideology of the entire history of humanity taken as a whole.
It is an appearance or ideology that cannot be “surpassed”—at least not by continuing in the same direction.
The socialist Phenomenology therefore describes how History as a whole “appears” to itself.
It describes the whole of History as a “phenomenon.”
And so we can say that its author exhausts not only his own capacity to understand the object but also the object itself insofar as it is his object.

For he gives an exhaustive description of the phenomenological side of the real dialectic insofar as that dialectic is realized—and has been realized—in the completed process of humanity’s historical, social, and political development.
That is why this Phenomenology can also be circular in the second, objective sense and therefore be objectively true.
By exhausting its own object, it certainly does not exhaust the phenomenological object in general.
Its object is only the historical or collective “appearance” of actuality. Actuality can still “appear” to human beings in another way: individually.
But the future dialectic of post-historical phenomena can no longer change the past dialectic of collective historical phenomena.
Their exhaustive description—the objectively circular description found in the socialist Phenomenology—can therefore be regarded as unchangeable, and thus as definitive or true.
Our Phenomenology, then, can be regarded as true.
And its truth is guaranteed by its circularity, and by nothing else.
What follows from the particular character of this truth?
If the truth of the Phenomenology is guaranteed by its circularity, then only the book as a whole can be fully convincing.

Taken in isolation, the description of any individual stage may seem arbitrary. Only when we understand how all the stages depend on one another do we become convinced that each individual description is correct.
That is why passages from the Phenomenology cannot properly be criticized when they are removed from the whole.
Strictly speaking, they cannot even be understood outside the whole, or if the whole itself is not understood.
For the dialectical character of an isolated element or moment becomes fully intelligible only through the place it occupies within the entire dialectical process.

To know or understand such an element means not only knowing what came before it—its “history,” its “becoming,” or its “origin”—but also knowing what comes after it, what develops out of it: its “goal,” its “tendency,” and its “result.”
But the whole does not merely provide the guarantee that the descriptions in the Phenomenology are true.
The truth itself revealed by the Phenomenology exists only in this whole.

As we already know, the Phenomenology is nothing other than a phenomenological anthropology: a discourse or science whose object is the human being, or more precisely the way human beings “appear” to themselves.
And this discourse claims to be true.
But it is obviously not the only discourse about humanity. Throughout its history, humanity has produced a vast range of theories about itself.
Why, then, should the truth belong only to the theory put forward by the author of the Phenomenology?
There can be only one answer.
The theory presented in the phenomenologist’s own name is certainly not an isolated theory existing alongside or against all the others.

The content of the phenomenologist’s theory is nothing other than the content of the Phenomenology itself, which consists precisely in describing absolutely all the theories about humanity that have appeared throughout the entire historical development of humanity.
There is therefore no need to choose between the phenomenologist’s theory and the theories produced throughout history, because the former contains all the others.
And if it is true, it is true precisely because it contains all of them—because there is no other possible theory that could be opposed to it, and nothing can be added to it that would change it.
In other words, every theory is true insofar as it “reveals” one aspect of actuality.
And every theory is false only insofar as it takes itself to “reveal” actuality as a whole.
Actuality as a whole is revealed only in the totality of all theories.
And since the Phenomenology is nothing other than such a totality, it is true in the strongest sense.
So when an isolated theory is completed by all the other theories—when its one-sidedness is destroyed—its falsity is destroyed as well, and the theory itself ceases to exist as an isolated theory.
The result of integrating all theories is one single, complete theory: an absolutely true theory, which is also the phenomenologist’s own theory.
And this complete, fully true theory is nothing other than the Phenomenology as a whole.
The Phenomenology is therefore true only as a whole—that is, as a closed circle.
In one sense, we can say that the phenomenologist “criticizes” isolated theories by completing them.
And if one wishes, one can say that he criticizes them from “his own” point of view.
But “his” point of view is nothing more than the sum of all points of view, including the very point of view he is criticizing.
So the points of view that seem to be criticized by the phenomenologist are in fact criticizing themselves.
Or, if you prefer, they criticize one another.
The Phenomenology merely records the result of this criticism as a process of self-criticism.
And the final result is the Phenomenology itself, in which this criticism or self-criticism is described.
But in saying this, we are clearly saying nothing new.

We are simply repeating that the phenomenologist restricts himself to a “pure description” of the real dialectical or historical process in which phenomena develop, generate their opposites while at the same time forming a unity with them, and in doing so are “dialectically overcome,” passing to an ever higher level.
The final level turns out to be the Phenomenology itself: the complete and exact description of the entire process of these dialectical overcomings.

In other words, the Phenomenology describes the process through which truth is progressively selected—the process we earlier described as the “technical” or “political” testing of “opinions” and “ideologies.”
And this description as a whole contains the total result of that testing.
It therefore contains all the truth and nothing but the truth.
Taken as a whole, the Phenomenology thus contains everything true, and in that sense it is entirely true.
But because the Phenomenology deals only with phenomena, the truth it contains concerns phenomena alone.
It shows only how the natural and human world “appears” to the human being who belongs to “history.”
To know what the world must be in order to “appear” in this way, we must move beyond the Phenomenology to Philosophy in the strict sense.
And this transition is possible only because the world’s “appearances” have been described exactly and exhaustively—that is, because the Phenomenology is completely and entirely true.
We have seen what the purpose of the Phenomenology is, what object it studies, and what method it uses to study that object and achieve its purpose.
So before presenting the Phenomenology itself, only one thing remains: to say something briefly about its structure.
On the one hand, we must explain why it necessarily divides into three basic parts and what is distinctive about each of them (2).
On the other hand, we must say a few words about the distinctive character of the work as a whole (3).

But since the structure of the Phenomenology is determined by its object, its method, and its purpose, as well as by the place it occupies within the general system of concrete knowledge, we must begin with this last question (1).
1. The place of Phenomenology within the system

In his investigation, or search for true knowledge, the philosopher begins with what is given to him “immediately”—that is, with what is given to him not as a “philosopher” but as an “ordinary” human being.
He therefore begins by clarifying and describing for himself how the natural and human world “appears” to humanity, and in particular how it appears to the people of his own age and to himself.
So he begins with a Phenomenology.
Only after he has taken into himself all these “appearances” of actuality does he move on to explaining their “cause” or their “conditions of possibility.”
Proceeding in this way, he first reaches the really existing natural-and-human world—the cosmos—and describes it in a Cosmology.
Only after completing that description does he arrive, in the end, at the ultimate or first “causes” of existence: being itself, which he describes in an Ontology.
He therefore moves from what is most “partial” and concrete—himself in his historical reality—to what is most “universal” and abstract: being as such.
